1.say: Read the last line of that paragraph. 'Mr Karimov was a man of few words. Most of them were no.' Why does it work? Because the second sentence is short and it comes last. Put it first and read them again. 'Most of them were no. Mr Karimov was a man of few words.' It is not funny any more. The joke is not in the words. It is in the order, and in the stop. Page two is worse. 'He read it twice. Then he signed. Once.' A one-word fragment, and the editor will want to join it to the line before. Should I let her? Not there. A fragment earns its place when it does something a whole sentence cannot, and 'once' is the entire point of the paragraph. And if I write four of them? Then none of them does anything, and the editor is right about all four.

grammar.label: the grammar of humour — timing, the turn and the last word
grammar.form: delayed disclosure; the deflating final clause; the register drop
grammar.meaning: puts the surprising element where it does the most work

explanation.en: A joke is a sentence whose end changes the meaning of its beginning, so word order is the whole craft. The surprising word goes last — 'I have nothing to declare but my genius' fails entirely as 'but my genius, I have nothing to declare'. Humour in a second language is the last thing to arrive because it depends on knowing exactly what the listener expects.
explanation.uz: Hazil — oxiri boshini o'zgartiradigan gap, shuning uchun so'z tartibi butun mahorat. Kutilmagan so'z oxirida turadi.

grammar.positive_example: He is a man of few words, and he has used most of them on me this morning.
grammar.negative_example: He has used most of his few words on me, being a man of few words this morning.

l1_notes.uz: Hazil kutilgan narsani bilishga bog'liq; bu esa chet tilida eng oxirida keladigan bilim.

grammar.label: deliberate rule-breaking — the sentence fragment and the one-word paragraph
grammar.form: a fragment used for emphasis; a paragraph of one sentence; a sentence opening with And or But
grammar.meaning: breaks a convention visibly, so the reader knows it was a choice

explanation.en: 'And that was that.' A fragment is an error when it is an accident and a device when it is not, and the only thing separating them is whether the rest of the text shows a writer in control. Break one rule on a page and it reads as style; break four and it reads as someone who does not know them.
explanation.uz: 'And that was that.' Tugallanmagan gap — tasodif bo'lsa xato, ataylab bo'lsa uslub. Ularni faqat matnning qolgan qismi ajratadi.

grammar.positive_example: The committee met for nine hours. Nine hours. And decided nothing.
grammar.negative_example: The committee met. For nine hours. Deciding. Nothing at all. Which was typical.

l1_notes.uz: Qoidani ataylab buzish — ingliz uslubining bir qismi, lekin faqat qolgan matn nazorat ostida ekani ko'rinsa.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Read the last line of that paragraph.

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: 'Mr Karimov was a man of few words. Most of them were no.'

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: Because the second sentence is short and it comes last.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Put it first and read them again.

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: 'Most of them were no. Mr Karimov was a man of few words.' It is not funny any more.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: The joke is not in the words. It is in the order, and in the stop.

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: Page two is worse. 'He read it twice. Then he signed. Once.'

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: A one-word fragment, and the editor will want to join it to the line before.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Not there. A fragment earns its place when it does something a whole sentence cannot, and 'once' is the entire point of the paragraph.

body.speaker: Dilnoza
body.text: And if I write four of them?

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: Then none of them does anything, and the editor is right about all four.
